en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
Naggavagga 25.
The Training Rule on the Transfer of Robes.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhunī, having gone for alms and spread out her wet robe, entered the vihāra.
Another bhikkhunī put on that robe and entered the village for alms.
Having emerged, she asked the bhikkhunīs:
“Sisters, would you look at my robe?
The bhikkhunīs informed that bhikkhunī of this matter.
Then that bhikkhunī complained, grumbled, and became indignant:
“How indeed can a bhikkhunī put on my robe without asking for permission?
Then that bhikkhunī informed the bhikkhunīs of this matter.
Those bhikkhunīs who were of few desires... [as before]... were indignant, complained, and grumbled:
“How indeed can a bhikkhunī put on a bhikkhunī’s robe without asking permission?
… [as before] … “Is it true, monks, that a bhikkhunī puts on a bhikkhunī’s robe without asking permission?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How, monks, can a bhikkhunī put on a robe without asking permission from another bhikkhunī?
This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so forth].
And thus, monks, let the bhikkhunīs recite this training rule:
“Whichever bhikkhunī should wear a robe that is to be passed on [to another], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Whichever bhikkhunī...
Whoever she may be, of whatever kind she may be …pe… “a bhikkhunī” …pe… this is the bhikkhunī intended in this context.
"Transferable robe-cloth" means:

if one wears or puts on as an upper garment any one of the five types of robes belonging to a person who is fully ordained, whether it has not been given to her or without having asked her permission, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one perceives a person who is fully ordained as being fully ordained, and she wears transferable robe-cloth, there is an offense of expiation.
If she wears a robe that should be exchanged with one who is fully ordained, while being in doubt as to whether she is fully ordained, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
If she wears a robe that should be exchanged with one who is fully ordained, perceiving her to be not fully ordained, there is an offense of expiation.
If she wears a robe that should be exchanged with one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If she perceives one who is not fully ordained as being fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she is doubtful regarding one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she perceives one who is not fully ordained as being not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense if she gives it herself, or if,
having asked her permission, one puts on the lower robe or the upper robe.
For one whose robe has been cut off,
for one whose robe has been lost,
and in times of distress.
"In the case of one who is insane,
or in the case of one who is a first-offender.
The fifth training rule is concluded.
